lessons.title: netfilter and nftables: default drop, allow, reject
lessons.goal:
Learn how the kernel's packet filter works, write nftables rules with a default-drop policy, and see the difference between DROP (silence) and REJECT (an answer).

Why it matters: a firewall mistake is either an outage (you block yourself) or a hole. Seeing the exact effect of each rule type prepares you for both.

setup.note: A client namespace `lab-c` (10.200.5.1) talks to a server namespace `lab-s` (10.200.5.2) that runs a small web server on port 8080. The firewall rules are written **inside `lab-s` only**, so your real firewall is not touched. Needs sudo, nft and curl.
commands: for n in lab-c lab-s; do sudo ip netns del $n 2>/dev/null; done; true
sudo ip netns add lab-c; sudo ip netns add lab-s; sudo ip link add vc type veth peer name vs; sudo ip link set vc netns lab-c; sudo ip link set vs netns lab-s

sudo ip -n lab-c addr add 10.200.5.1/24 dev vc; sudo ip -n lab-s addr add 10.200.5.2/24 dev vs; for n in lab-c lab-s; do sudo ip -n $n link set lo up; done; sudo ip -n lab-c link set vc up; sudo ip -n lab-s link set vs up

steps.title: netfilter and nftables
steps.text: **netfilter** is the kernel framework with **hooks** along the path of a packet (prerouting, input, forward, output, postrouting). Rules attached to those hooks can accept, drop, reject, modify or count packets. **nftables** (`nft`) is the modern way to write the rules; **iptables** is the older front end for the same hooks. A rule is stored in a **chain** inside a **table**; a chain declared with a hook and a **policy** is a *base chain*.

run.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-s python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 10.200.5.2 > /dev/null 2>&1 & echo $! > srv.pid; sleep 1; echo server started
sudo ip netns exec lab-c curl -s -m 2 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://10.200.5.2:8080/
sudo ip netns exec lab-s nft list ruleset | wc -l | awk '{print $1, "rules loaded in lab-s"}'

steps.title: Default drop
steps.text: We create a table and an `input` chain on the **input** hook (packets addressed to this host) with `policy drop`: anything not explicitly accepted is silently discarded. The client now gets no answer at all and times out.

run.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-s nft add table inet filter
sudo ip netns exec lab-s nft 'add chain inet filter input { type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop; }'
sudo ip netns exec lab-c curl -s -m 2 -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code} time=%{time_total}s\n' http://10.200.5.2:8080/; echo "curl exit code: $?"

steps.after: Exit code 28 means a timeout. From the client's side a dropped packet looks exactly like a dead host.

steps.title: Allow what is needed
steps.text: Typical base rules: accept replies to connections we started (`ct state established,related`), accept loopback, then the services you offer. Each rule can have a `counter`.

run.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-s nft add rule inet filter input ct state established,related accept
sudo ip netns exec lab-s nft add rule inet filter input iif lo accept
sudo ip netns exec lab-s nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 8080 counter accept
sudo ip netns exec lab-c curl -s -m 2 -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}\n' http://10.200.5.2:8080/

steps.title: The rule set and its counters
steps.text: `nft list ruleset` prints everything. The counter on the `tcp dport 8080` rule counted the packets of the new connection that matched it. Packets of the same connection afterwards match the `established` rule.

run.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-s nft list ruleset | sed -E 's/packets [0-9]+ bytes [0-9]+/packets N bytes N/'

steps.under: netfilter tracks connections with **conntrack**: the first packet of a flow is `new`, later ones are `established`. That is why one `established,related accept` rule suffices for return traffic, and why stateful firewalls cost memory (the conntrack table size is `net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max`).

steps.title: DROP versus REJECT
steps.text: `reject` sends back an error (TCP reset or ICMP unreachable), so the client fails **at once** with `Connection refused`. `drop` makes it wait for the full timeout. REJECT is friendlier for internal services, DROP gives scanners less information. We insert a reject rule above the accept rule.

run.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-s nft insert rule inet filter input tcp dport 8080 counter reject with tcp reset
sudo ip netns exec lab-c curl -s -m 5 -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code} time=%{time_total}s\n' http://10.200.5.2:8080/; echo "curl exit code: $?"

steps.after: Exit code 7 is `connection refused`, and it came back immediately (time near zero) instead of after 2 seconds.

steps.title: Clean up
steps.text: Stop the server and remove the namespaces.

run.cmd: sudo kill $(cat srv.pid) 2>/dev/null; sleep 0.3; for n in lab-c lab-s; do sudo ip netns del $n; done; echo removed

quiz.q: What does a base chain with `policy drop` do with packets no rule accepts?
What is the client's view of a DROP rule?
Why do firewalls usually start with `ct state established,related accept`?
options: Replies to connections you opened and related traffic must be allowed back
quiz.explain: Return traffic would otherwise be dropped.

quiz.q: Which tool is the modern front end for netfilter?

check.scenario: You are logged in over SSH and must tighten the firewall to default-drop remotely. How do you avoid locking yourself out?
check.answer: Put the `accept` rules for SSH (and `established,related`) in place **before** switching the policy to drop, apply the change with an automatic rollback (`nft -f new.rules` inside `timeout 60 ... || nft -f old.rules`, or `at now + 2 minutes` to flush), test in a second session, and keep console access.

lessons.title: NAT with nftables, iptables compatibility and firewalld
lessons.goal:
Publish a server behind a router with destination NAT (port forwarding), see that `iptables` rules are stored by nftables underneath, and read a firewalld configuration.

Why it matters: port forwarding, masquerading and container networking are all NAT rules. firewalld is the default front end on Red Hat systems, so you need to read what it generates.

setup.note: These steps reuse the three-namespace lab: lab-a (10.200.1.1) - lab-b, a router with two addresses - lab-c (10.200.2.2). A web server runs in lab-c; the router publishes it on its own address with NAT. The last step reads (and does not change) the real firewalld of this machine. Needs sudo, nft and curl.
commands: for n in lab-a lab-b lab-c; do sudo ip netns del $n 2>/dev/null; done; true
for n in lab-a lab-b lab-c; do sudo ip netns add $n; sudo ip -n $n link set lo up; done
sudo ip link add va type veth peer name vb1; sudo ip link set va netns lab-a; sudo ip link set vb1 netns lab-b
sudo ip link add vb2 type veth peer name vc; sudo ip link set vb2 netns lab-b; sudo ip link set vc netns lab-c
sudo ip -n lab-a addr add 10.200.1.1/24 dev va; sudo ip -n lab-b addr add 10.200.1.2/24 dev vb1; sudo ip -n lab-b addr add 10.200.2.1/24 dev vb2; sudo ip -n lab-c addr add 10.200.2.2/24 dev vc
sudo ip -n lab-a link set va up; sudo ip -n lab-b link set vb1 up; sudo ip -n lab-b link set vb2 up; sudo ip -n lab-c link set vc up
sudo ip netns exec lab-b sysctl -qw net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
sudo ip -n lab-a route add 10.200.2.0/24 via 10.200.1.2; sudo ip -n lab-c route add 10.200.1.0/24 via 10.200.2.1

steps.title: The server behind the router
steps.text: The web server listens on `lab-c` (10.200.2.2:8080). `lab-a` can reach it directly because `lab-b` routes. We want `lab-a` to reach it through the router's address instead: `10.200.1.2:9090`.

run.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-c python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 10.200.2.2 > /dev/null 2>&1 & echo $! > srv.pid; sleep 1
sudo ip netns exec lab-a curl -s -m 2 -o /dev/null -w 'direct: http=%{http_code}\n' http://10.200.2.2:8080/
sudo ip netns exec lab-a curl -s -m 2 -o /dev/null -w 'via router: http=%{http_code}\n' http://10.200.1.2:9090/; echo "curl exit code: $?"
run.output:
via router: http=000
curl exit code: 7

steps.title: Destination NAT (port forwarding)
steps.text: A rule in the **prerouting** hook of a `nat` table rewrites the destination of arriving packets **before** the routing decision. Packets for `10.200.1.2:9090` get the new destination `10.200.2.2:8080`. The kernel remembers the translation in conntrack and rewrites the replies back automatically.

run.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-b nft add table ip nat
sudo ip netns exec lab-b nft 'add chain ip nat prerouting { type nat hook prerouting priority -100; }'
sudo ip netns exec lab-b nft add rule ip nat prerouting ip daddr 10.200.1.2 tcp dport 9090 counter dnat to 10.200.2.2:8080
sudo ip netns exec lab-a curl -s -m 2 -o /dev/null -w 'via router: http=%{http_code}\n' http://10.200.1.2:9090/

steps.under: The packet is never rewritten again by you: conntrack stores the original and translated tuples. The reply from 10.200.2.2:8080 is translated back to 10.200.1.2:9090 on its way out, so the client believes it talked to the router. **Source NAT / masquerade** does the opposite for outgoing traffic: it rewrites the source address to the router's public one (how a home router or a container host shares one address).

steps.title: See the translation
steps.text: The conntrack table lists the original and the reply direction of each tracked flow, if the tool is installed. The nftables counter proves the rule matched.

run.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-b nft list ruleset | sed -E 's/packets [0-9]+ bytes [0-9]+/packets N bytes N/'
sudo ip netns exec lab-b cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count 2>/dev/null | awk '{print "tracked flows in lab-b:", ($1 >= 0)}'

steps.title: iptables is a front end for the same hooks
steps.text: On current distributions `iptables` is a compatibility program that translates its rules into nftables. A rule added with `iptables` therefore shows up in `nft list ruleset`.

run.cmd: iptables --version | sed -E 's/ v[0-9.]+//'
sudo ip netns exec lab-b iptables -A FORWARD -p tcp --dport 8080 -j ACCEPT; sudo ip netns exec lab-b iptables -S FORWARD
run.output:
-P FORWARD ACCEPT
-A FORWARD -p tcp -m tcp --dport 8080 -j ACCEPT

run.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-b nft list ruleset | grep -B1 -A4 'chain FORWARD' | head -n 7

steps.title: firewalld: the usual front end
steps.text: firewalld groups interfaces into **zones**, each with allowed services and ports. It generates nftables rules. Changes have a **runtime** and a **permanent** configuration. We only read this machine's firewall.

run.cmd: sudo firewall-cmd --state
sudo firewall-cmd --get-default-zone
sudo firewall-cmd --list-services
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8080/tcp && sudo firewall-cmd --reload
run.reason: it would open a port on this machine; shown as the command you would run

steps.title: Clean up
steps.text: Stop the server and remove the namespaces.

run.cmd: sudo kill $(cat srv.pid) 2>/dev/null; sleep 0.3; for n in lab-a lab-b lab-c; do sudo ip netns del $n; done; ip netns list | wc -l | awk '{print $1, "namespaces left"}'

quiz.q: Which hook is used for destination NAT (port forwarding)?
quiz.explain: Before routing, so the new destination is routed.

options: Rewrites the source address of outgoing packets to the outgoing interface's address

quiz.q: Where do rules added with `iptables` end up on a modern system?
Which command line shows firewalld's active zones and their rules?

check.scenario: A container published with `-p 8080:80` is reachable from the host but not from other machines. Where do you look?
check.answer: At the host's firewall: the **FORWARD** and the **INPUT/zone** rules (firewalld zone, `iptables -S`/`nft list ruleset` for DOCKER chains), `net.ipv4.ip_forward`, whether the port is bound to `127.0.0.1` only (`ss -ltnp`), and the cloud security group. Check the NAT rule exists (`nft list table ip nat` or `iptables -t nat -S`) and watch counters while testing.

interview.a: The packet-filtering framework in the Linux kernel: hooks on the packet path where rules (nftables/iptables) can accept, drop, modify or track packets. See [the lesson](#/lesson/31/netfilter-nftables).
nftables is the current framework (one tool, sets, atomic rule replacement). iptables is a compatibility front end that now creates nftables rules.
DROP discards silently (client waits for a timeout). REJECT sends an error (reset or ICMP), so the client fails immediately.

interview.q: How do you write a safe default-deny firewall?
interview.a: Accept established/related, loopback and the services you offer first; then set policy drop. Keep a way back (console, timed rollback). See [the lesson](#/lesson/31/netfilter-nftables).

DNAT rewrites the destination (port forwarding) in prerouting; SNAT/masquerade rewrites the source (sharing an address) in postrouting. Conntrack translates replies back. See [the NAT lesson](#/lesson/31/nat-and-firewalld).

interview.q: How does firewalld relate to nftables?
interview.a: firewalld is a manager with zones, services and runtime/permanent config; it generates nftables rules. Do not mix manual nft rules with firewalld unless you know the order.

glossary.def: The kernel's packet-filtering and NAT framework.
The current tool and rule language for netfilter.
An ordered list of rules in a table; a base chain is attached to a hook.
Connection tracking: the kernel table that remembers flows for stateful rules and NAT.
Destination NAT: rewriting the destination of packets (port forwarding).
Source NAT using the address of the outgoing interface.
A firewall manager with zones, services and runtime/permanent configuration.

commands.cmd: sudo nft add table inet filter
sudo nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 accept

commands.desc: List iptables rules in command form.
